extracted.intended_audience: historians and students of the history and philosophy of science; scholars studying Francis Bacon's Novum Organum and experimental method
extracted.subtask_description: Exegesis and practical extraction of Bacon's experimental-method criteria (the Instantiae taxonomy, seven operative modes, canons of predominance, and concrete experimental prescriptions) from Novum Organum with commentary and examples. Focused on how to design, classify, and interpret experiments/instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Innuentes (Intimating Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which intimate or suggest what is profitable to human uses; they point to directions for experiments and operations that matter most to human concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their office is to 'dirigere operativam ad ea quae maxime hominum intersunt.' In interpretation of particular subjects the author assigns them a place in the 'Charta Humana' or 'Charta Optativa'. They amplify human power (posse) and knowledge (scire) and show profitable practical directions; collect them carefully to guide operative inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Polychrestae (Multipurpose / Frequently Occurring Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that pertain to varied and often-recurrent cases and therefore repay continual testing and application; often include instruments, processes, or contrivances usable across many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polychrestae should be collected and tested thoroughly; they overlap with Instantiae Radii and Curriculi and will be treated more fully with instruments and modes of experiment. Examples include materials and methods for excluding air, sealing vessels, conservation techniques, and commonly-applicable contrivances; record them in Historiis Particularibus and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of impeding/disturbing agents (exclusiones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or exclude those things (e.g., common air, celestial rays) that disturb or impede the operation under study so as to isolate the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical means: choice of vessel materials and thickness; accurate methods of obturation/sealing (consolidation and 'luhim sapientiae'); covering liquids (e.g., oil over wine) to form a protecting layer; powders and viscous coatings (wax, pitch, wax/ceres, honey) to exclude air; subterranean storages and immersion (placing objects at the bottom of waters) to exclude insolation and open air; use of dense metals or media (e.g., work 'intra argentum vivum') to shield. These are treated as polychrestic techniques and should be experimented with for preservation or enabling interior operations (for example, to prevent spirits exiting a body while operating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compressions, extensions, agitations and similar violences
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying violent mechanical actions (compression, extension, agitation) as powerful agents to produce local motion, transformations, or destruction (in machines and organic bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression is especially potent: it can stop combustion, destroy life, alter machines and organic structures, and change colors/flavors when parts become more dissimilar. But such violent means often produce only transient effects tending to recoil/restitution; to test whether compression produces a permanent change one must design experiments with delay and auxiliaries (e.g., compressing water, then allowing a long rest to see if a new consistent state remains). Suggested experiments: compressing/hammering water or gases in vessels and testing after days; condensing air in glass eggs then sealing and leaving for days before testing for permanent rarefaction/condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat and cold as operative instruments (calidum et frigidum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ temperature extremes (heat and cold) deliberately to operate on bodies; recognize practical asymmetries (heat is abundant, cold scarce) and seek or create instances of cold for useful transformations (condensation, transmutations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cold is relatively rare and must be sought in towers, subterranean caverns, snow/ice surrounds, deep wells, burial in quicksilver/metals, immersion in waters, etc. Investigate natural cold-induced condensations (dew, exudation of marble, subterranean vapour collections) to transfer their causes to art. Consider pharmacological condensants (astringents, soporifics) and two modes of condensation of spirits (by sedation of motion or by flight/fugation). Look for 'succedanea' of cold (substitutes) and modes that produce condensation without raw cold (i.e., via mixtures or other artificial means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of delay in a convenient place (mora in loco convenienti)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying time (prolonged rest or delay) as an operative factor to effect or reveal transformations which do not occur instantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments where after applying a violent or altering treatment the specimen is allowed to rest for days, weeks, or longer before inspecting for permanence (e.g., compressed water allowed to 'plana' then extracted; glass eggs evacuated, firmly sealed and left for days before testing whether air returns with a hiss or the same quantity of water is drawn upon immersion). If effects persist after delay they may be genuine transformations; if they revert they were transient. Use delay both alone and in combination with auxiliaries/consensus to attempt to make transient changes permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraenum et regimen motus (restraint and regulation of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control, bridle or regulate motion as an operative means to influence outcomes of processes and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint/regulation can be used to limit or direct motions that would otherwise lead to restitution or undesired effects; examples include binding limbs to observe attempts at resurgence (to see if 'nixus' continues despite apparent failure). Consider how limiting degrees of freedom or applying constraints change the course of reactions or mechanical behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus speciales (special unions/adhesions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of special adhesions, unions or cooperative agents between parts (chemical or mechanical 'consensus') to produce effects not attainable by single agents alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These include adhesives, medicaments that attract or bind spirits, and artificial associations of parts; test how special consensuses assist in making transient changes durable, or in producing new properties (e.g., medicines that condense spirits by inviting vapors to unite). Use consensus as an auxiliary with compression, heat/cold, and delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation, timely succession, and series of operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply operations in particular sequences and timely alternations; the order and timing (series/succession) of interventions matter for producing and stabilizing effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimenters must consider series and succession of the seven operative modes or of auxiliaries (e.g., compress → delay → consensus) and test different timings; some transformations require alternation or a specific sequence to become permanent. Record and systematize successful series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canones praedominantiae (canons/rules for collecting predominance in conflicts of forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and analyze instances of conflict (luctae) to determine which force or motion predominates under given conditions; derive general canons of predominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of canons: the more common or universal the 'good' aimed at, the stronger the motivating motion; motus nexus (motions respecting the communion of the universe) may be stronger than motus gravitatis (motions respecting communion of the dense bodies); private appetites rarely prevail against public ones except in small quantities. To discover these canons collect instances of struggles, compare their quantitative and qualitative relations, and derive rules indicating when one cause will predominate or succumb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative experiments to reveal concurrent or counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Design comparative trials to distinguish the full operation of a cause from effects masked by concurrent or counteracting causes; compare conditions where causes concur vs oppose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: a cause operates to its full efficiency even when its effect is not apparent due to other causes. Example experiment proposed: determine the 'point-blank' range of a gun and then fire at that range first upwards (where Motus Ictus is simple) then downwards (where Motus Gravitatis concurs) to compare the force — this reveals how concurrent motives alter observed effect. More generally, use comparative arrangements (concurrence vs opposition) to isolate contributions of different motions or factors.
